name: Ottoman Empire
tierReason: A mighty gunpowder army, but powerful rivals in Europe and Persia demand careful balance.
summary: Take Constantinople, face the Safavids, and hold a giant empire of many faiths together.
intro: You begin as Sultan Mehmed II in 1453 and guide the Ottoman Empire through the reigns of Selim I, Suleiman the Magnificent, and beyond. Your strengths: an elite army armed with gunpowder weapons, and lands that sit between Europe and Asia. Your challenges: rivals on every border and millions of subjects of many different faiths to hold together.

collapse.text: Too many costly mistakes left your treasury empty, your soldiers unpaid, and your provinces in revolt. Rival empires carved up your lands.

survive.text: Your empire endures to 1750 as one of the great powers of Europe, Asia, and Africa.

glossary.def: the ruler of the Ottoman Empire
the Eastern Roman Empire, a Christian empire centered on Constantinople
the sultan's elite infantry soldiers, armed with muskets
taking Christian boys from Balkan villages, converting them to Islam, and training them as soldiers or officials loyal only to the sultan
letting each religious community run its own affairs under its own leaders
Turkmen tribal cavalry loyal to the Safavid shah, named for their red caps
a sultanate ruled by former slave-soldiers that controlled Egypt and Syria
law codes issued by the sultan to work alongside Islamic religious law
an alliance of Christian powers, mostly Catholic, organized with the Pope's support
selling the right to collect taxes to private collectors, who kept anything extra they squeezed out

timeline.text: Mehmed II conquers Constantinople with giant cannons. The city becomes the Ottoman capital, Istanbul.
Selim I defeats the Shia Safavids at Chaldiran, then conquers Mamluk Egypt and becomes protector of Mecca and Medina.
Suleiman the Magnificent wins at Mohács, besieges Vienna (1529), and issues law codes. Sinan builds the Süleymaniye Mosque.
After decades of janissary revolts and money troubles, the Köprülü grand viziers restore order.
A failed second siege of Vienna leads to the Treaty of Karlowitz, the first major permanent loss of Ottoman land to European powers.
Leaders begin borrowing European ideas, including the first Ottoman Turkish printing press. The empire lasts until 1922.

constantinople.title: The Walls of Constantinople
constantinople.text: You are Sultan Mehmed II, just 21 years old. Constantinople, the capital of what is left of the old Byzantine Empire, sits in the middle of your lands and controls trade between Europe and Asia. Its thousand-year-old walls have stopped attackers for centuries. An engineer from Hungary named Orban offers to build you some of the biggest cannons the world has ever seen.

options.text: Hire Orban, cast giant bronze cannons, and attack the city by land and sea at the same time.
options.explanation: Brilliant—this is what Mehmed did. Orban's cannons pounded the walls for weeks, Ottoman ships were even dragged overland into the city's harbor, and Constantinople fell on May 29, 1453. Big guns like these are one reason historians call the Ottomans a "gunpowder empire."

options.text: Surround the city and wait for it to starve. No need to risk an attack.
options.explanation: Patient, but slow. A blockade alone could take years, because Venetian and Genoese ships could slip in supplies by sea. Mehmed won quickly in 1453 by combining a blockade with massive cannon fire and a final assault.

options.text: Leave the city alone and conquer easier lands in Anatolia instead.
options.explanation: A missed opportunity. An enemy capital in the heart of your empire could become a base for European crusades. Mehmed made Constantinople his first target, and its capture in 1453 shocked Europe and made his reputation.

walls.title: The City Still Stands
walls.text: Two years later, Constantinople still holds out. Venetian ships keep slipping in supplies, and the Pope is calling on Europe's kings to send a crusade to defend the city. Your generals are restless, and rivals at court whisper that you are weak.

options.text: Build Orban's giant cannons now and launch a combined attack by land and sea.
options.explanation: Better late than never. Heavy cannons were the key to breaking walls like these. In reality, Mehmed didn't wait: he used this approach in 1453, and the city fell after a siege of about 53 days.

options.text: Throw wave after wave of foot soldiers at the walls until they break.
options.explanation: Costly. Attacking walls this strong without heavy cannons would waste thousands of soldiers. Mehmed's success in 1453 came from pairing big guns with well-timed assaults.

options.text: Offer the Byzantine emperor safe passage if he surrenders the city peacefully.
options.explanation: Worth a try—Mehmed actually made an offer like this in 1453. Emperor Constantine XI refused and died defending the city, so Mehmed still needed his cannons and a final assault.

istanbul.title: A City of Many Faiths
istanbul.text: Constantinople is yours, and you make it your capital (it will become known as Istanbul). But the city is half-empty, and your empire now rules millions of Orthodox Christians, plus smaller Jewish and Armenian communities, alongside Muslims. As a Muslim ruler, how will you govern so many different peoples?

options.text: Let each religious community run its own affairs under its own leaders, as long as they stay loyal and pay the jizya tax. Bring people of all faiths to resettle the city.
options.explanation: Excellent. Mehmed named a new Orthodox patriarch, resettled the city with Muslims, Christians, and Jews (many of them moved there by force), and turned the great Hagia Sophia church into a mosque. This approach, later called the millet system, kept diverse subjects loyal and paying taxes for centuries.

options.text: Order every Christian and Jew to convert to Islam or leave.
options.explanation: Risky and costly. Forced conversion would spark revolts and drive away the merchants and craftsmen your new capital needed. Mehmed did the opposite: he protected non-Muslim communities in exchange for taxes and loyalty.

options.text: Fill the city only with Muslim Turkish settlers and push non-Muslims out to the countryside.
options.explanation: Partly workable, but you would lose skilled Greek, Armenian, and Jewish merchants and artisans. Mehmed deliberately resettled people of many faiths in the city, and Istanbul grew into one of the largest and most diverse cities in the world.

chaldiran.title: Showdown at Chaldiran
chaldiran.text: It is 1514, and you are now Sultan Selim I. To the east, Shah Ismail of the new Safavid Empire in Persia has made Shia Islam his official religion, and his preachers are winning followers among Turkmen tribes inside your lands. The Ottomans are Sunni Muslims, so you see this as a threat to your faith and your throne. Ismail's Qizilbash cavalry are fearsome horsemen, while your janissaries were recruited as boys through the devshirme.

context.text: Constantinople fell to you only after a long, expensive delay, and that cost you money and prestige.
Ever since Constantinople, your army has invested heavily in cannons and muskets.
Your army never fully embraced heavy cannons. It still relies mostly on cavalry.

options.text: March east and fight with your musket-armed janissaries and cannons chained together behind a wall of wagons.
options.explanation: A crushing victory—this is exactly what happened at the Battle of Chaldiran in 1514. Ottoman guns tore apart the Qizilbash cavalry, and Selim briefly captured the Safavid capital, Tabriz. The battle stopped Safavid expansion into Ottoman lands and locked the two empires into a long Sunni–Shia rivalry.

options.text: Buy cannons and hire gunners in a hurry, then march east with your janissaries.
options.explanation: It works, but barely in time. At the real Battle of Chaldiran in 1514, Selim's army already had plenty of cannons and musket-armed janissaries, and their firepower destroyed the Qizilbash cavalry. Investing in gunpowder earlier would have made this much easier.

options.text: Build forts along the border and stay on the defensive.
options.explanation: Safe but passive. Ismail's preachers would keep stirring up rebellion inside your lands. Selim chose to attack, and his victory at Chaldiran in 1514 stopped Safavid expansion into Anatolia.

options.text: Propose an alliance with Shah Ismail against the Christian kingdoms of Europe.
options.explanation: Unrealistic. The Sunni–Shia split made the two empires bitter rivals, and Ismail wanted to win your subjects over to his side. Instead, Selim defeated Ismail at the Battle of Chaldiran in 1514.

egypt.title: Egypt and the Holy Cities
egypt.text: With the Safavids beaten, you turn south. The Mamluk Sultanate rules Syria, Egypt, and the holy cities of Mecca and Medina. Egypt is rich in grain and taxes, and whoever protects Mecca and Medina gains enormous prestige among Sunni Muslims. The Mamluks are proud horsemen who still look down on guns.

options.text: Conquer the Mamluks and become the protector of Mecca and Medina.
options.explanation: Exactly right. Selim conquered Syria and Egypt in 1516–1517, again thanks to cannons and muskets. Guarding the holy cities gave Ottoman sultans huge religious legitimacy, and they sometimes used the title caliph, leader of the Muslim community.

options.text: Sign a friendship treaty with the Mamluks and trade with them.
options.explanation: Peaceful, but you would miss a huge prize. Egypt's grain and taxes, plus guardianship of the holy cities, made the Ottomans the leading Sunni power. Selim conquered the Mamluks in 1516–1517.

options.text: Skip Egypt and attack Hungary in Europe right away.
options.explanation: Europe would come later. Selim secured the Middle East first by conquering Syria and Egypt in 1516–1517, and his son Suleiman then crushed Hungary at the Battle of Mohács in 1526.

anatolia.title: Rebels in Anatolia
anatolia.text: Without a decisive win over the Safavids, Shah Ismail's influence keeps spreading. Turkmen tribes in eastern Anatolia wear the red caps of the Qizilbash and call Ismail their spiritual leader. Some villages refuse to pay your taxes at all.

options.text: Launch a new campaign east with your best janissaries and cannons, and win back the border.
options.explanation: Strong recovery. Ottoman firepower was far superior to Safavid cavalry in open battle. Historically, Selim won this showdown at Chaldiran in 1514 and secured eastern Anatolia.

options.text: Hunt down and punish anyone suspected of supporting the Shah.
options.explanation: Harsh and only partly effective. Selim really did persecute suspected Safavid supporters, but repression alone couldn't stop Ismail. What settled the matter was Selim's victory at Chaldiran in 1514.

options.text: Ignore the east. It's too far away to matter.
options.explanation: Dangerous. A rival empire winning over your own subjects is a direct threat to your throne. Selim took it seriously and crushed the Safavids at Chaldiran in 1514.

vienna.title: Suleiman at the Gates of Vienna
vienna.text: You are now Suleiman the Magnificent. You have already crushed the Kingdom of Hungary at the Battle of Mohács (1526). Now your huge army is camped outside Vienna, capital of the Habsburgs. But it's autumn, heavy rains forced you to leave your biggest cannons behind, and your supply lines stretch back hundreds of miles.

context.text: With Egypt's taxes and the prestige of protecting Mecca and Medina, your treasury and reputation are at their peak.

options.text: Pull back before winter, keep Hungary as a buffer under a friendly local king, and build an alliance with France, the Habsburgs' enemy.
options.explanation: Smart and realistic. Suleiman lifted the siege in October 1529 because winter and supply problems made victory impossible, and he left most of Hungary under a friendly vassal king, John Zápolya, while the Habsburgs held the rest. He later allied with France (1536) to pressure the Habsburgs.

options.text: Dig in and keep the siege going all winter, no matter the cost.
options.explanation: A disaster waiting to happen. Your army would starve and freeze far from home while the Habsburgs gathered reinforcements. Suleiman wisely retreated in October 1529.

options.text: Retreat, then turn to the sea: build a powerful navy to rule the Mediterranean.
options.explanation: A good long-term idea. Suleiman did build a strong navy under the admiral Hayreddin Barbarossa, which won the Battle of Preveza in 1538 and dominated much of the Mediterranean. He also had to govern the huge empire he had built, which is why Turks later nicknamed him Kanuni, "the Lawgiver."

lawgiver.title: Suleiman the Lawgiver
lawgiver.text: Your empire stretches from Hungary to Iraq and from the Black Sea to North Africa. Ruling it takes more than soldiers. Your officials need clear rules, and your subjects need reasons to see your rule as just and legitimate.

context.text: Letting religious communities run their own affairs has kept your Christian and Jewish subjects loyal taxpayers.
Your harsh treatment of non-Muslims back in Istanbul has left some Christian provinces in the Balkans restless.

options.text: Issue clear law codes (kanun) that work alongside Islamic law, promote officials for talent, and have the architect Sinan build magnificent mosques.
options.explanation: This is why Turks later called him Suleiman the Lawgiver. He expanded older kanun law codes and built a trained bureaucracy, and monuments like Sinan's Süleymaniye Mosque in Istanbul (finished 1557) showed that his rule was just, Islamic, and powerful.

options.text: Let each provincial governor make his own rules, as long as the taxes arrive.
options.explanation: Cheap but dangerous, because governors with their own rules can become rival powers. Suleiman did the opposite, issuing empire-wide law codes and sending trained officials to govern.

options.text: Spend everything on more wars. Laws and buildings can wait.
options.explanation: Wars without good government drain the treasury and anger the people who pay for them. Suleiman fought many wars, but he also invested in laws, officials, and monuments like the Süleymaniye Mosque that legitimized his rule.

overstretched.title: War on Two Fronts
overstretched.text: Your failed winter siege of Vienna cost thousands of soldiers. Now the Habsburgs are pushing back in Hungary, and in the east the Safavids are raiding Ottoman lands again. Your treasury is shrinking, and soldiers are grumbling about late pay.

options.text: Make peace with the Safavids so you can focus on Europe.
options.explanation: Wise. Fighting two great rivals at once is how empires break. Suleiman eventually signed the Peace of Amasya with the Safavids in 1555, which settled the border for decades.

options.text: Fight both enemies at full strength at the same time.
options.explanation: Too much at once. Campaigns on two distant fronts drained money and soldiers even for the mighty Ottomans. Suleiman switched between fronts and made peace with the Safavids in 1555.

options.text: Raise taxes sharply on peasants to pay for the armies.
options.explanation: Short-term cash, long-term anger. Heavy taxes, along with war, drought, and unpaid soldiers, helped spark the Celali revolts around 1600. Peace on one front, as with the Safavids in 1555, was a better way to save money.

navy.title: Disaster at Lepanto
navy.text: Suleiman died in 1566, and his son Selim II now rules. Your navy, built up by the great admiral Barbarossa, has ruled much of the Mediterranean for decades. But in 1571, a Holy League of Spain, Venice, and the Pope destroys most of your fleet at the Battle of Lepanto. Europe celebrates. Your ships are gone, but you still hold the island of Cyprus, which you just took from Venice.

options.text: Rebuild the fleet immediately and make peace with Venice on good terms.
options.explanation: Exactly what happened. The Ottomans rebuilt a fleet of more than 150 ships within a year, and Venice signed a peace in 1573 that let the Ottomans keep Cyprus. Lepanto was a famous defeat, but it did not end Ottoman power at sea.

options.text: Give up on the sea and focus only on land.
options.explanation: That would hand the Mediterranean to Spain and Venice and leave your coasts and trade unprotected. The Ottomans instead rebuilt their fleet within a year and kept Cyprus in the 1573 peace.

options.text: Spend everything on revenge: invade Spain itself.
options.explanation: Far too ambitious. Spain was across the entire Mediterranean, and a revenge invasion would have bankrupted you. The Ottomans rebuilt their fleet and made peace with Venice in 1573.

janissaries.title: The Janissaries Grow Too Powerful
janissaries.text: By the 1600s, things have changed. Fewer boys are taken through the devshirme, and janissaries now marry, run shops, and pass their jobs to their sons. Silver from the Americas and the government's own debasing of its coins (mixing in cheaper metal) have caused inflation, so soldiers' pay buys less. In 1622, mutinous janissaries killed Sultan Osman II, who had planned to replace them. The empire needs order.

context.text: Suleiman's law codes and trained officials still give your government a strong foundation.

options.text: Give real power to a capable grand vizier who can punish corruption, fix the finances, and restore discipline.
options.explanation: This is what worked. Starting in 1656, the Köprülü family of grand viziers restored order, crushed revolts, and even won new territory. Strong ministers kept the empire powerful even under weak sultans.

options.text: Abolish the janissaries overnight and build a brand-new army.
options.explanation: Osman II tried something like this and was murdered by the janissaries in 1622. Getting rid of such a powerful group took careful preparation, and the Ottomans did not manage it until 1826.

options.text: Keep the janissaries happy with bonuses, paid for by selling tax-collecting rights to the highest bidder.
options.explanation: This is close to what happened, and it bought time. But tax farming let collectors squeeze peasants, and payoffs didn't fix discipline. Real recovery came when the Köprülü grand viziers took charge in 1656.

vienna1683.title: Vienna, Once More
vienna1683.text: The Köprülü viziers have restored order, and the army feels strong again. Grand Vizier Kara Mustafa wants glory: he plans to march a huge army to Vienna and finish what Suleiman started in 1529, even though a twenty-year peace treaty with the Habsburgs has not quite run out. Europe's Catholic powers are watching nervously.

options.text: Keep the peace, strengthen your borders, and invest in the army and treasury instead.
options.explanation: The wise choice. Kara Mustafa's real siege of Vienna in 1683 ended in disaster when a Polish-led relief army attacked. In the long war that followed, the Ottomans lost most of Hungary in the Treaty of Karlowitz (1699).

options.text: March on Vienna with the biggest army possible, just as Kara Mustafa wants.
options.explanation: This is what really happened, and it went badly. A relief army led by King Jan Sobieski of Poland crushed the Ottomans outside Vienna in 1683, and a Holy League pushed them out of most of Hungary. The Treaty of Karlowitz (1699) was the first time the Ottomans permanently gave up large territories to European powers.

options.text: Attack Vienna, but move fast, bring your heaviest cannons, and guard against a relief army.
options.explanation: Better planned, but still a gamble. In 1683 the siege dragged on for two months, giving Europe time to send a relief army. The defeat led to the loss of most of Hungary in the Treaty of Karlowitz (1699).

karlowitz.title: The Treaty of Karlowitz
karlowitz.text: Without firm leadership at home, your army has lost its discipline. After a failed siege of Vienna in 1683, a Holy League of Austria, Poland, Venice, and Russia has beaten you again and again. European armies now drill with better muskets and tactics. Your diplomats are offered a peace treaty, but it means giving up most of Hungary and other lands for good.

options.text: Sign the treaty, then study European military methods and ideas like printing books in Turkish.
options.explanation: Realistic and forward-looking. The Ottomans signed the Treaty of Karlowitz in 1699, and in the early 1700s some leaders began borrowing European ideas, including the first Ottoman Turkish printing press in the late 1720s. The empire survived for two more centuries.

options.text: Refuse the treaty and keep fighting every enemy at once.

collapse.text: Fighting Austria, Russia, Poland, and Venice all at once was more than your exhausted army and empty treasury could bear. Provinces broke away, and enemy armies marched deep into your lands.

options.explanation: Pride over survival. In reality, the Ottomans signed the Treaty of Karlowitz in 1699 and lived to fight another day; the empire lasted until 1922.

options.text: Sign the treaty, but blame and execute your generals instead of changing anything.
options.explanation: Blaming individuals doesn't fix an army that is falling behind. The Ottomans signed the treaty in 1699, and later reformers argued that the empire had to learn from Europe, leading to experiments like the first Ottoman Turkish printing press in the late 1720s.
